Notebook 04: Preprocessing Pipeline¶

Objectives¶

In this notebook we develop and validate the preprocessing pipeline for the PANORAMA pancreatic CT dataset.

The goals are:

  • Load CT volumes using the reusable src package
  • Inspect CT intensity distributions
  • Perform Hounsfield Unit (HU) clipping
  • Normalize CT intensities
  • Resample all scans to a common voxel spacing
  • Prepare processed volumes for model training

Unlike the previous notebooks, this notebook focuses on image preprocessing rather than dataset exploration.

Section 2: Inspect CT Intensity Distribution¶

CT images are stored in Hounsfield Units (HU), where each voxel represents the X-ray attenuation of tissue.

Typical HU values include:

Tissue Approximate HU
Air -1000
Lung -700
Fat -100
Water 0
Soft tissue 30–80
Bone 300–3000

Before applying any preprocessing, we first inspect the intensity distribution of one CT scan. This helps us understand the dynamic range of the data and motivates later steps such as HU clipping and normalization.

Observations¶

The CT volume contains a wide range of Hounsfield Unit values, from approximately -1024 HU (air) to over 3000 HU (dense bone or metal).

Most voxels are concentrated within the soft-tissue range, while extreme values occupy relatively few voxels.

Because neural networks do not benefit from these extreme intensities, the next preprocessing step will clip the CT volume to a fixed HU window before normalization.

Section 3: Hounsfield Unit Clipping¶

CT images contain a wide range of intensity values. However, pancreatic tissue occupies only a small portion of this range.

Very low values (air and background) and very high values (bone and metallic objects) contribute little useful information for pancreatic cancer detection and may negatively affect neural network training.

Therefore, CT intensities are clipped to a soft-tissue window before normalization.

For this project we use:

  • Lower bound: -150 HU
  • Upper bound: 250 HU

These values preserve pancreatic anatomy while suppressing irrelevant intensity extremes.

print()

print("Clipped range")
print(clipped.min(), clipped.max())

lower = -150
upper = 250

below = np.sum(image < lower)

above = np.sum(image > upper)

total = image.size

print(f"Below {lower} HU : {below:,}")

print(f"Above {upper} HU : {above:,}")

print(f"Total voxels     : {total:,}")

print()

print(f"Below (%) : {100*below/total:.2f}%")

print(f"Above (%) : {100*above/total:.2f}%")

Below -150 HU : 11,746,389
Above 250 HU : 401,872
Total voxels     : 23,592,960

Below (%) : 49.79%
Above (%) : 1.70%

Observations¶

HU clipping removes extreme intensity values while preserving the majority of soft tissue.

Most of the modified voxels correspond to background air and dense bone.

This operation reduces the dynamic range of CT intensities and prepares the images for normalization, improving numerical stability during deep learning model training.
